svg.title: Fig. 2 - How vitamin letters accumulated (1912-1940s)
svg.desc: Bands for fat-soluble and water-soluble factors with approximate naming decades; letters are historical labels, not supplement instructions.
svg.text: How A, B-complex members, C, D, E, and K entered the vocabulary - many provisional letters retired.
McCollum & Osborne-Mendel rat work - A (1920) - D (calciferol era) - E (Evans) - K (Dam & Doisy)
Sterol chemistry (Windaus) sits under D; irradiation patents (Steenbock/WARF) are commerce, not clinical copy.
Letters name fractions before structures are final - the map is messy on purpose.
B-complex splits: thiamine (B1), riboflavin, niacin, B6, biotin, pantothenic, folate, B12 - each with its own bench story.
C: hexuronic acid - ascorbic acid (Szent-Gy-rgyi, Haworth). Funk's 1912 guess about amines was wrong; the nickname stuck.
Suzuki's oryzanin (Japan) parallels bran work - same rice polish, different publication language.
Japanese and European threads meet in journals, not in a single "inventor" line.
Retired provisional letters (F, G, H, ...) - naming collisions resolved by chemistry, not marketing.
History-of-science diagram. Not a Supplement Facts panel.
